messages.author: 98ca4936e74d2d4f
messages.subject: Backward angles
parts:
Dear DISTANCE freaks,
for one-sided boat transects (e.g. left side) we haven normally the
situation that birds get detected within 'forward' angels 0-90 degrees, but
sometimes we have detections within 'backward' angles 90-180 degrees, e.g.
when a bird comes to the surface behind the boat, or a bird get detected
once the boat has passed by already.

For recording angle and direct distance of an object, instead of
perpendicular distance, I like to know how to deal best with these 'backward
angle' cases .
Thanks and best regards
Falk

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: Backward angles
parts:
> > for one-sided boat transects (e.g. left side) we haven normally the
> > situation that birds get detected within 'forward' angels 0-90 degrees, but
> > sometimes we have detections within 'backward' angles 90-180 degrees, e.g.
> > when a bird comes to the surface behind the boat, or a bird get detected
> > once the boat has passed by already.
> >
> > For recording angle and direct distance of an object, instead of
> > perpendicular distance, I like to know how to deal best with these 'backward
> > angle' cases .

Unless the bird flew in after you passed the spot, then it is generally
better to treat such detections just like any other. Distance from the
line can be calculated as sighting distance * sin(sighting angle), exactly
as for forward angles. For diving birds especially, this helps to ensure
that prob of detection on or near the trackline is close to unity, as
required for standard line transect sampling.

Steve Buckland
